title: Git Time Travel: Cherry-pick, Bisect & Reflog
summary: A dense field guide to moving commits between branches, hunting down the commit that broke things, and recovering work Git appears to have lost. Covers the object model underneath these commands, their mechanics, real command sequences, trade-offs against alternatives, and the mistakes that bite people in practice.

chapters.title: Commits, DAGs and the Three Tools
points: A commit is an immutable snapshot object: tree SHA + parent SHA(s) + author/committer + message; the SHA-1/SHA-256 hash covers all of it
History is a directed acyclic graph, not a line: a branch is a movable pointer to one commit; HEAD points to a branch (or directly to a commit when detached)
Because parent and metadata are hashed in, 'moving' a commit is impossible — cherry-pick and rebase always create a NEW commit with a new SHA
Definition: cherry-pick = replay the diff of one (or a range of) commit onto the current HEAD
Definition: bisect = binary search over the commit DAG to find the first commit where a property flipped (usually good→bad)
Definition: reflog = a local, per-ref journal of every value HEAD and each branch has pointed at, with timestamps
The tool triad maps to three questions: 'I want this change here' (cherry-pick), 'which change caused this' (bisect), 'where did my commit go' (reflog)
Reachability vs existence: an object can exist in .git/objects while unreachable from any branch — reflog is what keeps it reachable, and gc is what eventually deletes it
Terminology trap: 'lost commits' are almost never lost until `git gc` runs; the default reflog expiry is 90 days (30 for unreachable entries)
Mental model for the whole handbook: patches (content diffs) vs pointers (refs) vs history (the DAG) — each command touches a different one

chapters.title: Cherry-pick: Replaying a Commit Elsewhere
points: `git cherry-pick <sha>` computes the diff of <sha> against its parent and applies it as a three-way merge onto HEAD, then commits with the original message and author
New commit gets a new SHA, a new committer date, and a new parent — original author and author-date are preserved
Range form: `git cherry-pick A..B` picks everything after A up to B; `A^..B` includes A itself — off-by-one here is the classic mistake
`-n` / `--no-commit` stages the change without committing, so you can pick several and squash them into one commit
`-x` appends '(cherry picked from commit <sha>)' to the message — essential for release branches and backports so provenance is traceable
`-e` edits the message; `-s` adds Signed-off-by; `--ff` fast-forwards instead of creating a new commit when HEAD is the picked commit's parent
`-m 1` is required to cherry-pick a merge commit: it names which parent to diff against (mainline), because a merge has no single unambiguous diff
Example backport: `git checkout release-1.4 && git cherry-pick -x 9fceb02 && git push origin release-1.4`
Conflict flow: fix files, `git add`, then `git cherry-pick --continue`; abandon with `--abort` (restores pre-pick state) or `--skip` (drops just that commit)
`git cherry-pick --continue` reuses the stored message from .git/sequencer — you do not re-specify the commit
`git cherry -v upstream branch` lists which of your commits are NOT yet upstream (equivalent patch-id matching), the read-only companion to picking

chapters.title: Cherry-pick vs Merge vs Rebase vs Revert
points: Merge: joins two histories with a merge commit; Git records the relationship so the same change is never applied twice
Cherry-pick: copies content only; Git records NO relationship, so the change exists twice under two SHAs
Consequence — 'duplicate commit' problem: if you cherry-pick from a feature branch and later merge that branch, the same patch arrives twice and may conflict
Git's patch-id matching (used by rebase and `git cherry`) usually detects and drops already-applied duplicates, but only if the patch text is byte-identical
Rebase = cherry-pick applied in a loop over a range, plus moving the branch pointer at the end (`git rebase` literally uses the same sequencer machinery)
Revert: creates a NEW commit that applies the inverse diff — it does not delete history, so it is the safe choice on shared branches

`git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>` reverts a merge; the notorious follow-up trap is that re-merging that branch later brings back nothing, since the merge base already claims it merged — you must revert the revert
Comparison row — when to cherry-pick: hotfix backport to a maintenance branch, salvaging one commit from an abandoned branch, applying a fix before a big refactor lands
Comparison row — when NOT to cherry-pick: pulling in a whole feature (merge instead), reordering your own unpushed work (interactive rebase instead)
Rule of thumb: cherry-pick across long-lived branches that will never merge; merge across branches that will
Trade-off table: history fidelity (merge: high, cherry-pick: low), conflict cost (merge: once, cherry-pick: every branch), auditability (revert: best on public history)

chapters.title: Bisect: Binary Search Over History
points: Problem it solves: a bug appeared somewhere in N commits and you do not know where; linear checking is O(N), bisect is O(log2 N)
300 commits ≈ 9 test runs; 10,000 commits ≈ 14 runs — the log scale is why bisect beats intuition even on huge ranges
Core assumption: the property is monotonic — once bad, always bad. Flaky tests and intermittent bugs break bisect's correctness
Session: `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad` (current, broken), `git bisect good <old-sha>` (known working); Git checks out a midpoint in detached HEAD
At each step you test, then say `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`; `git bisect skip` marks a commit untestable (broken build) and Git picks a neighbour
Git prints 'roughly N steps' and finally 'X is the first bad commit' plus the full commit display
`git bisect reset` returns to the original branch and ref; `git bisect log` dumps the session, `git bisect replay <file>` re-runs it after a mistake
`git bisect visualize` (or `view`) opens gitk/log on the remaining suspect range
Mechanism on a DAG: with merges, the 'midpoint' is the commit that best halves the number of ancestors still suspect — bisect handles non-linear history natively
`git bisect start --term-old=fast --term-new=slow` renames the terms for non-bug hunts, e.g. performance regressions or 'when did this feature appear'
Example range shortcut: `git bisect start HEAD v2.3.0` sets bad and good in one command

chapters.title: Automated Bisect and Bisect in Anger
points: `git bisect run <cmd>` automates the whole search: exit 0 = good, exit 1-124/126/127 excluded, exit 125 = skip (untestable), any other 1-127 = bad
Exit code 125 is the reserved 'cannot test this commit' signal — return it from your script when the build fails for unrelated reasons
Example: `git bisect run npm test -- tests/checkout.spec.js`
Example with a script: `git bisect run ./bisect-check.sh` where the script builds, runs one assertion, and exits 125 if the build fails
One-liner probe: `git bisect run sh -c 'make -j8 || exit 125; ./app --selftest'`
Grep-based probe for 'when did this string appear': `git bisect run sh -c '! grep -q deprecatedCall src/api.ts'`
Keep the test script OUTSIDE the repo (or in /tmp) — checking out old commits replaces or deletes a script that lives in the tree
Dependency drift: old commits may need old lockfiles; add `npm ci` / `pip install -r requirements.txt` to the script or you bisect your node_modules, not your code
`git bisect run` combined with `git bisect skip` ranges can end with 'the first bad commit could be any of' — several candidates, because skipped commits were never tested
Cost trade-off: automation pays off when the test is fast and deterministic; a 20-minute build over 12 steps is 4 hours — narrow the range with `git log -S` first
`git log -S'symbol'` (pickaxe) and `git log -L` are faster than bisect when you already know which line or symbol changed

chapters.title: Reflog: The Local Undo Journal
points: `git reflog` (short for `git reflog show HEAD`) lists every position HEAD has held: checkout, commit, reset, rebase, merge, pull — each with a reason string
Syntax `HEAD@{n}` means 'n moves ago'; `HEAD@{2.hours.ago}` and `HEAD@{yesterday}` select by time — distinct from `HEAD~n`, which means 'n commits back in the DAG'
Per-branch reflogs exist too: `git reflog show main`, selector `main@{1}` = where main pointed before its last update
Storage: plain append-only text at .git/logs/HEAD and .git/logs/refs/heads/<branch> — old-sha new-sha author timestamp\treason
Reflog is strictly LOCAL and never pushed, fetched, or cloned; a fresh clone has a one-line reflog
Expiry defaults: gc.reflogExpire 90 days for reachable entries, gc.reflogExpireUnreachable 30 days; `git gc --prune=now` after that removes the objects for real
Recover a deleted branch: `git reflog` to find the tip SHA, then `git branch recovered <sha>`
Undo a bad `git reset --hard`: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`
Undo a botched rebase: `git reset --hard <branch>@{1}` — or use ORIG_HEAD, which Git sets before reset, merge, and rebase
Recover a dropped stash: stashes leave reflog entries under refs/stash — `git fsck --unreachable | grep commit` finds truly orphaned ones
Reflog vs `git fsck --lost-found`: reflog covers ref movements; fsck finds dangling objects even when no ref ever pointed at them (e.g. an aborted commit)
`git reflog expire --expire=now --all` deliberately destroys the safety net — only used before a genuine `gc --prune=now` cleanup

chapters.title: Recovery Playbooks: When Things Go Wrong
points: Playbook — amended away a commit: `git reflog`, find the pre-amend SHA, `git cherry-pick <sha>` or `git reset --hard <sha>`
Playbook — force-pushed over a colleague's work: their commits still live in YOUR reflog only if you had them; otherwise ask them, or check the remote's `git reflog` on the server if you host it
Playbook — deleted branch after merge, need it back: `git reflog | grep <branch-name>` finds the last checkout entry
Playbook — rebase went sideways mid-way: `git rebase --abort` first; if already finished, `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD`
Playbook — cherry-picked onto the wrong branch: `git reset --hard HEAD~1` on the wrong branch, then re-pick on the right one (the source commit is untouched)
Playbook — bisect left you detached and confused: `git bisect reset` always restores the branch you started from
`--force-with-lease` instead of `--force` refuses the push if the remote moved — the cheapest way to avoid needing these playbooks
Safety habit: before any history rewrite, `git branch backup/$(date +%s)` costs nothing and beats reflog archaeology
`git fsck --full --no-reflogs --unreachable --lost-found` writes orphaned commits into .git/lost-found for inspection

Understand the destructive triad: `reset --hard` (working tree + index + HEAD), `checkout -- .` (working tree only), `clean -fd` (untracked files) — only the first is reflog-recoverable, uncommitted work is NOT in the reflog at all
Hard rule: the reflog cannot recover changes you never committed or stashed — commit early, even garbage commits, if you are about to do something risky

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Trade-offs
points: Mistake: cherry-picking a commit that depends on an earlier commit — the pick applies cleanly but the code is broken at runtime because a helper it calls does not exist yet
Mistake: cherry-picking without `-x` on a release branch, then no one can trace which upstream fix it corresponds to
Mistake: forgetting `A^..B` and losing commit A from a picked range
Mistake: bisecting a flaky test — you get a confidently wrong 'first bad commit'; run the test several times per step or mark flaky ones with `skip`
Mistake: bisecting with a stale build cache or stale node_modules so every step tests the same artifacts
Mistake: assuming the reflog exists on a fresh clone or in CI — it does not, so 'just use the reflog' is not a recovery plan for automated environments
Mistake: confusing `HEAD@{1}` (previous ref position) with `HEAD~1` (parent commit) — different answers whenever HEAD moved without committing
Mistake: running `git gc --prune=now` or `git reflog expire --all` to 'clean up', destroying the recovery window
Trade-off: heavy cherry-picking makes release branches diverge in content while looking related — later merges conflict repeatedly on the same hunks
Trade-off: bisect gives you the commit, not the cause — a large squashed commit narrows the search to 800 lines, which is why small commits pay off here
Trade-off: `--first-parent` bisect (`git bisect start --first-parent`) blames the merge, not the individual commit — faster on merge-heavy history, less precise
Anti-pattern: using cherry-pick as a substitute for a proper merge strategy across long-lived branches — the duplication debt compounds every release

chapters.title: Command Cheatsheet
points: Cherry-pick: `git cherry-pick <sha>` | range `A^..B` | `-n` no commit | `-x` record source | `-e` edit msg | `-m 1` merge commit | `--continue` / `--abort` / `--skip`
Find what to pick: `git cherry -v upstream topic` lists unmerged commits; `git log --oneline --no-merges main..topic`
Bisect: `git bisect start` → `bad` → `good <sha>` → test → `good`/`bad`/`skip` → `git bisect reset`
Bisect fast path: `git bisect start HEAD v1.9 && git bisect run ./check.sh` (exit 0 good, 1 bad, 125 skip)
Bisect session control: `git bisect log > b.log`, `git bisect replay b.log`, `git bisect visualize`, `--term-old`/`--term-new`
Reflog: `git reflog` | `git reflog show <branch>` | `HEAD@{n}` | `<branch>@{1}` | `HEAD@{2.days.ago}`
Undo: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` (last move) | `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` (before reset/merge/rebase) | `git branch rescue <sha>`
Orphan hunt: `git fsck --full --unreachable --lost-found` | `git show <dangling-sha>`
Search instead of bisect: `git log -S'string'` (pickaxe) | `git log -L :func:file.c` | `git log --oneline -- path/`
Safety: `git push --force-with-lease` | `git branch backup-$(date +%s)` before rewrites | never `gc --prune=now` while investigating
Config knobs: `gc.reflogExpire=90.days`, `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable=30.days`, `core.logAllRefUpdates=true` (must be on for reflog to exist)
Decision line: copy one change → cherry-pick; find the breaking change → bisect; get something back → reflog; undo public history → revert
